## Multilevel Curve of Factors with categorical indicators

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
This is the second part of a lecture on multilevel approaches to modeling growth. This is a useful strategy when there are a lot of repeated observations. 

This lecture builds on part 1 by treating the observed variables as categorical, rather than continuous.

I will run the following models:<br>
1. Continuous variable CFA [(model21, CFA Continuous)](#CFAContinuous)<br>
2. Categorical variable CFA [(model22, CFA Categorical)](#CFACategorical)<br>
3. Categorical variable CFA with covariates[(model23, CFA Categorical)](#CFACategoricalwithCovariates)<br>
4. Multiple indicator latent growth curve model [(model24, MILGCM)](#MILGCM)<br>
5. Multilevel curve of factors [(model25, MLCOF)](#MLCOF)
:::

### Data

As in the previous example: this example uses data that are Centers for Epidemiologic Studies - Depression (CESD) scale responses collected from the New Haven Site of the EPESE (Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly) study. In this lecture, the four-category responses of six CESD questions will be treated as categorical  indicators of a common underlying trait.

These data are public and can be obtained from ICPSR.

```{r}
#| label: MplusEngine

knitr::knit_engines$set(mplus = function(options) {
    code <- paste(options$code, collapse = "\n")
    fileConn<-file("formplus.inp")
    writeLines(code, fileConn)
    close(fileConn)
    out  <- system2("/Applications/Mplus/mplus", "formplus.inp")
    fileConnOutput <- file("formplus.out")
    mplusOutput <- readLines(fileConnOutput)
    knitr::engine_output(options, code, mplusOutput)
})
```

<!-- readSvalues function thanks ChatGPT -->
```{r}
#| label: readSvaluesfunction
#| echo: false 
#| output: false 
readSvalues <- function(filename) {
  # Read the file lines into a vector
  lines <- readLines(filename)
  
  # Initialize an empty vector to store the lines of interest
  lines_of_interest <- character(0)
  
  # Flag to keep track of whether the starting line has been found
  found_start <- FALSE
  # Counter for blank lines
  blank_line_count <- 0
  
  # Loop through each line in the file
  for (line in lines) {
    # Check for the starting line
    if (grepl("MODEL COMMAND WITH FINAL ESTIMATES USED AS STARTING VALUES", line)) {
      found_start <- TRUE
      next
    }
    
    # If the starting line has been found, process the lines until 3 blank lines are encountered
    if (found_start) {
      if (nchar(trimws(line)) == 0) { # Check for a blank line
        blank_line_count <- blank_line_count + 1
        if (blank_line_count == 3) {
          break
        }
      } else {
        blank_line_count <- 0 # Reset blank line counter if a non-blank line is found
        lines_of_interest <- c(lines_of_interest, line) # Add the line to the vector
      }
    }
  }
  
  # Remove blank lines from the lines of interest
  lines_of_interest <- lines_of_interest[nchar(trimws(lines_of_interest)) > 0]
  
  # Return the character vector
  return(lines_of_interest)
}
```

<!-- itemsummary thanks ChatGPT -->
```{r}
#| label: itemsummary function
#| echo: false
#| output: false

# Load necessary packages
if (!requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("dplyr")
if (!requireNamespace("tidyr", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("tidyr")

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Define the function
itemsummary <- function(data, vars) {
  # Melt the data frame to long format with variable-value pairs
  long_data <- pivot_longer(data, cols = all_of(vars), values_to = "Values", names_to = "Variable")
  
  # Replace actual NA with a character "NA" for counting
  long_data$Values <- replace_na(as.character(long_data$Values), "NA")
  
  # Count occurrences of each value for each variable
  frequency_data <- long_data %>%
    group_by(Variable, Values) %>%
    summarise(Frequency = n(), .groups = 'drop')
  
  # Spread the frequency data to wide format
  wide_frequency_data <- pivot_wider(frequency_data, names_from = Values, values_from = Frequency, values_fill = list(Frequency = 0))
  
  return(wide_frequency_data)
}

# Example usage
# Assuming 'df' is your data frame and you have variables 'var1', 'var2', 'var3', etc.
# consolidated_table <- createConsolidatedFrequencyTable(df, c("var1", "var2", "var3"))
# print(consolidated_table)


```

Note: CES-D items are asked with a past week look-back, and response categories have the labels: rarely or none of the time (less than 1 day); some or a little of the time (1-2 days); occasionally or a moderate amount of time (3-4 days); and most or all of the time (5-7 days). Category labels are reversed for positive items (*enjoy*, *happy*,  *hopeful*).

# Continuous item CFA of CESD at baseline

```{mplus}
TITLE:    Continuous item CFA of CESD at baseline
DATA:     FILE = cesditems.dat ;
VARIABLE: NAMES = sad blues depress happy enjoy hopeful; 
          MISSING = . ;
MODEL:    f by sad@1 blues-hopeful*;
OUTPUT:   STDYX  ;
```

# Mplus Multiple Indicator LGC model, categorical items

<!-- Data set up in multilevel-Curve-of-factors.qmd -->
<!-- DATA:     FILE = "cesdwide.dat"; -->
<!-- VARIABLE: NAMES = id female agec70  -->
<!--           y01 y02 y03 y04 y05 y06  -->

<!--           y61 y62 y63 y64 y65 y66;  -->

## MILGCM {#MILGCM}

```{r}
#| label: l544_showme_model1
showme("402-model24.inp")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
**Note:**  Data set up in "Multilevel Curve of Factors" presentation.
:::


---

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
Note in this model we have:
:::

```
MODEL:    f0 by u01@1.281 u02-u06* (l1-l6); ! = 1.24246*sqrt(1.063)
          f3 by u31@1.281 u32-u36* (l1-l6); ! where 1.063 is estimate in TECH4
          f6 by u61@1.281 u62-u66* (l1-l6); ! of VAR(F0) when l1 = 1.24246
```

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
On the first run of this mode, the variance of `f0` was 1.063 in the TECH4
output. It should be exected that the constraint on `u01` or `sad` derived 
from the one time point model would not perfectly produce a 1.0 variance in 
the longitudinal model. The longitudinal model we have forces equal residual
variance on the time-specific latent traits (`f0`, `f3`, and `f6`) and these
will come out as a weighted average. It is not reasonable to assume this
parameter would be the same as the model that only included f1. Also, 
the `f3` and `f6` factors are predicted by latent variable `S`, but 
`f0` is not. 

The implication of this is we could probably have skipped the three step
procedure using the baseline model to get a latent variable variance of 1 
in the MILGCM and just run two MILGM models (as was done here).

You will see in this model, the TECH4 variance estimate for `f0` is 1.0.
:::
------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{mplus}
TITLE:    Categorical item multiple indicator LGCM of CESD
DATA:     FILE = "cesdwide.dat";
VARIABLE: NAMES = id female agec70 
          u01 u02 u03 u04 u05 u06 
          u31 u32 u33 u34 u35 u36 
          u61 u62 u63 u64 u65 u66; 
          IDVARIABLE = id ;
          MISSING = . ;
          CATEGORICAL are u01-u66 ;
ANALYSIS: ESTIMATOR = MLR ; LINK = PROBIT ;
MODEL:    f0 by u01@1.281 u02-u06* (l1-l6); ! = 1.24246*sqrt(1.063)
          f3 by u31@1.281 u32-u36* (l1-l6); ! where 1.063 is estimate
          f6 by u61@1.281 u62-u66* (l1-l6); ! of VAR(F0) when l1 = 1.24246
          f0 f3 f6 (psi) ; ! for comparability with MLGOF
          ! Also no item-level resid covar for comparability with MLGOF
          [u01$1 u31$1 u61$1] (t11) ;
          [u01$2 u31$2 u61$2] (t12) ;
          [u01$3 u31$3 u61$3] (t13) ;                  
          [u02$1 u32$1 u62$1] (t21) ;
          [u02$2 u32$2 u62$2] (t22) ;
          [u02$3 u32$3 u62$3] (t23) ;                  
          [u03$1 u33$1 u63$1] (t31) ;
          [u03$2 u33$2 u63$2] (t32) ;
          [u03$3 u33$3 u63$3] (t33) ;                  
          [u04$1 u34$1 u64$1] (t41) ;
          [u04$2 u34$2 u64$2] (t42) ;
          [u04$3 u34$3 u64$3] (t43) ;                  
          [u05$1 u35$1 u65$1] (t51) ;
          [u05$2 u35$2 u65$2] (t52) ;
          [u05$3 u35$3 u65$3] (t53) ;                  
          [u06$1 u36$1 u66$1] (t61) ;
          [u06$2 u36$2 u66$2] (t62) ;
          [u06$3 u36$3 u66$3] (t63) ;
          i by f0@1 f3@1 f6@1 ;
          i* ;
          [i@0] ;
          s by f0@0 f3@0.3 f6@0.6 ;
          s* ;
          [s*] ;
          i with s ;
          i s on female agec70 ;
OUTPUT: TECH4;
```

# Mplus Multilevel Growth of Factors, categorical items


## MLCOF {#MLGOF}

```{r}
#| label: l629_showme_model1
showme("402-model25.inp")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
Note: The scale for `fw` :
:::
```
MODEL:    %WITHIN%
          fw by sad@1.281 blues-hopeful*; 
```

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}

Was borrowed from the MILGM model. It was not possible to run TECH4 in `model25.inp`, the MLCOF model. Mplus says:

:::

```
*** WARNING in OUTPUT command
  TECH4 option is only available for TYPE=TWOLEVEL RANDOM with ESTIMATOR=BAYES.
  Request for TECH4 is ignored.
```

::: {style="font-size:0.5em;"}
Switching to `ESTIMATOR=BAYES` is therefore an option, but even `tho I am using 
one of three common scale parameterizations (MLR/PROBIT) and the parameter estimates
will be on the same scale in MLR/PROBIT and BAYES, they might not be equal 
enough to guarantee a variance of 1 at the first time point. But it is an option.

Also, if I have a follow-up model to run that includes sampling weights, that 
cannot be accommodated by `ESTIMATOR=BAYES`. 

Therefore I also can't confirm the variance of `fw` is 1.0 at baseline
without calculating the variance "by hand" or moving to a Bayes estimator.

:::



---

```{mplus}
TITLE:    Categorical item multilevel growth of factors ;
DATA:     FILE = cesdlongk.dat ;
          VARIANCES = NOCHECK ;
VARIABLE: NAMES = id td female agec70 sad blues depress happy enjoy hopeful k ; 
          CATEGORICAL are sad blues depress happy enjoy hopeful ;
          MISSING = . ;
          WITHIN = td k ;
          BETWEEN = agec70 female ; 
          CLUSTER = id ;
ANALYSIS: TYPE = TWOLEVEL RANDOM ;
          ESTIMATOR = MLR ; 
          LINK = PROBIT ;
MODEL:    %WITHIN%
          fw by sad@1.281 blues-hopeful*; 
          s | fw on td ;
          i | fw on k ;
          %BETWEEN%
          !sad-hopeful@0 ; ! This would be included in continuous variable case
          [i@0] ;
          i with s ;
          i s on female agec70 ;
```

## Summary

::: {style="font-size:0.6em;"}
The multiple indicator latent growth curve model (MILGCM) and multilevel growth of factors (MLGOF) models for categorical variables are equivalent, with some constraints (no item level residual covariances in MILGCM; equal residual variances for time-specific common factors in MIGCM).


```{r}
#| label: l41_process_output
#| echo: false
milgmResults <- MplusAutomation::readModels(target="402-model24.out")
milgmParameters <-  milgmResults$parameters$unstandardized %>% mutate(PARAMETER = str_c(paramHeader,param, sep = " "))
mlcofResults <- MplusAutomation::readModels(target="402-model25.out")
mlcofParameters <-  mlcofResults$parameters$unstandardized %>% mutate(PARAMETER = str_c(paramHeader,param, sep = " "))
# Elapsed time
timePattern <- "\\d{2}:\\d{2}:\\d{2}"
milgmElapsedTime <- regmatches(grep("Elapsed Time:", milgmResults$output, value = TRUE), regexpr(timePattern, grep("Elapsed Time:", milgmResults$output, value = TRUE)))
mlcofElapsedTime <- regmatches(grep("Elapsed Time:", mlcofResults$output, value = TRUE), regexpr(timePattern, grep("Elapsed Time:", mlcofResults$output, value = TRUE)))

```


| **Parameter** | **MILGCM** | **MLCOF** | 
|:--|--:|--:|
|Number of free parameters | `r milgmResults$summaries$Parameters`                          | `r mlcofResults$summaries$Parameters`         |
|Loglikelihood             | `r sprintf("%.3f", milgmResults$summaries$LL)`                 | `r sprintf("%.3f", mlcofResults$summaries$LL)` |
|Correction factor         | `r sprintf("%.3f", milgmResults$summaries$LLCorrectionFactor)` | `r sprintf("%.3f", mlcofResults$summaries$LLCorrectionFactor)` |
|I with S                  | `r milgmParameters$est[milgmParameters$PARAMETER == "I.WITH S"]`|`r mlcofParameters$est[mlcofParameters$PARAMETER == "I.WITH S"]`|
|Intercept(I)              |@0|@0|
|Intercept(S)              |`r milgmParameters$est[milgmParameters$PARAMETER == "Intercepts S"]`|`r mlcofParameters$est[mlcofParameters$PARAMETER == "Intercepts S"]`|
